stops.name: Mecca, the flight home, the cloak of Khadija, the words of Waraqa
stops.campa: He comes down the mountain trembling, his heart beating hard, and reaches Khadija crying, Cover me, cover me! She wraps him until the fear leaves, then says: God will never disgrace you; you keep good relations, bear the burdens of others, speak the truth. She takes him to her cousin Waraqa, an old blind Christian who knows the scriptures, and Waraqa declares: This is the Namus that came to Moses. Would that I were young when your people drive you out. Driven out? he asks. Yes, Waraqa says: no man brought the like without being fought.
stops.quote: This is the Namus (Gabriel) whom Allah sent to Moses. I wish I were young and could live up to the time when your people would turn you out. Would they drive me out? Yes, never came a man with the like of what you have brought but was treated with hostility.

stops.name: Mecca, the first believers: Khadija, Ali, Abu Bakr, Zayd
stops.campa: The Word continues to descend, and the first hands are stretched out to it. Khadija believes before any other, the first of all the ummah. Ali, the boy of the house whom the Prophet raised, believes though still a child; Zayd, the freed servant and adopted son, believes; and among the men Abu Bakr, whose word carries weight in Mecca, believes at once and brings others after him. They pray in secret in the ravines and houses of Mecca, a hidden congregation, while the idols still stand in the House.

stops.name: Mecca, the open call and the persecution of the Quraysh
stops.campa: Commanded to proclaim openly, he climbs Mount Safa and warns his clans of the Reckoning, and calls them from many gods to the One. The Quraysh, fearing for the House and their trade, turn on him. They mock, they throw filth as he prays, they set the entrails of a slaughtered camel on his back at the Kaaba; his daughter comes weeping to clean him. The weak among the believers are seized and beaten. Yet the recitation keeps descending, and the little band holds, praying toward the House.
stops.quote: Proclaim what you are commanded, and turn away from the polytheists. Indeed, We are sufficient for you against the mockers.

stops.name: Mecca, Bilal on the burning sands, 'One! One!'
stops.campa: Bilal the Abyssinian, slave of Umayya ibn Khalaf, will not renounce the One God. His master drags him out into the noon of Mecca, throws him on the scorching sand, and lays a great rock upon his chest to crush the faith from him. Through the heat Bilal answers only, Ahad, Ahad: One, One. Abu Bakr passes, sees the torment, and buys him free. So the tortured slave becomes a freedman of the faith, and one day his voice, first of all voices, will call the prayer from the roof of the Kaaba.
stops.quote_source: Ibn Ishaq, Sirat Rasul Allah (the trial of Bilal)

stops.name: Aksum, the emigration to Abyssinia and the court of the Negus
stops.campa: As the persecution hardens, the Messenger sends a band of the weak across the sea to the Christian king of Abyssinia, the Negus, a just ruler under whom none is wronged. When the Quraysh send envoys demanding the refugees back, the Negus summons them; Ja'far, cousin of the Prophet, speaks for the faith and recites the sura of Mary: the words on Jesus and his virgin mother. The king weeps into his beard and marks a line on the ground: what you have brought and what Jesus brought come from one lamp. He shelters them, and will not give them up.
stops.quote: This and what Jesus brought have come from the same niche of light. Go, for you are safe in my land; I will not give you up.
stops.quote_source: Ibn Ishaq, Sirat Rasul Allah (the first migration to Abyssinia)

stops.name: Mecca, the ravine of Abu Talib, the three-year boycott
stops.campa: The Quraysh hang a written pact in the Kaaba: none shall trade with, marry, or speak to the Banu Hashim until they surrender the Prophet. For nearly three years the clan is penned in the ravine of Abu Talib, hungry, the cries of the children heard beyond the rocks, sustained only by what friends can smuggle in. Then the Prophet tells his uncle that God has sent a creeping thing upon the document and eaten all but the name of God. They open the Kaaba; it is as he said, and the shamed chiefs tear the boycott down.

stops.name: Mecca, the Year of Sorrow, the deaths of Khadija and Abu Talib
stops.campa: In one bitter year the two who sheltered him are taken. Khadija dies, the first believer, the wife of twenty-five years, in whose love he found rest and in whose arms he wept his first fear. And Abu Talib dies, the uncle who guarded him from the Quraysh though he never spoke the creed. Grief lies heavy on the Messenger; the year is named the Year of Sorrow. The protection about him is stripped away, and the Quraysh grow bolder against him now that the old lion is gone.

stops.name: Ta'if, the stoning and the supplication
stops.campa: Seeking new ground for the faith, he goes up to Ta'if in the cool hills with Zayd. The chiefs rebuff him and set the slaves and boys to line the road and pelt him with stones until his sandals fill with blood. Bruised, he shelters in a garden and lifts a supplication of pure surrender: to You I complain of my weakness; if You are not angry with me I do not care. Gabriel comes with the angel of the mountains, offering to crush the two hills of Mecca upon them. He refuses: rather, that God bring from their loins a people who worship Him alone.
stops.quote: O Allah, to You I complain of my weakness, my scarcity of resources, and my lowliness before men. You are the Lord of the weak, and You are my Lord. If You are not angry with me I do not care, but Your protection is more expansive for me.
stops.quote_source: The Supplication of Ta'if (Ibn Ishaq; al-Tabarani)

stops.name: Mecca, the Sacred Mosque, Buraq and the start of the Night Journey
stops.campa: As he lies near the Kaaba, in the place called al-Hijr, Gabriel comes and splits his breast once more, washing the heart with Zamzam and filling it with faith and wisdom. Then is brought Buraq, a white beast smaller than a mule and larger than an ass, whose stride reaches as far as its eye can see. Mounted upon it, with Gabriel beside him, the Messenger is carried in a single night out of the Sacred Mosque and northward over the sleeping earth, toward the Farthest Mosque at Jerusalem. Glory be to Him who took His servant by night.
stops.quote: Glory be to Him who took His servant by night from the Sacred Mosque to the Farthest Mosque, whose surroundings We have blessed, to show him of Our signs.

stops.name: Jerusalem, the Farthest Mosque, the Prophet leads the prophets in prayer
stops.campa: Buraq alights at the Noble Sanctuary, at the Rock from which Solomon's Temple rose, and the Messenger tethers the beast at the ring where the prophets tied theirs. He enters the Farthest Mosque, and there the messengers of God are gathered: Abraham, Moses, Jesus and all the rest. Gabriel sets him forward, and Muhammad leads the whole assembly of prophets in prayer, imam of them all. Two vessels are offered him, wine and milk; he chooses the milk, and Gabriel says: you have chosen the right nature, the fitrah, for your people.

stops.name: The Seven Heavens, the ascent past the prophets (the Mi'raj)
stops.campa: From the Rock, upon a ladder of light, the ascent begins. At the first heaven's gate stands Adam, father of mankind, greeting his righteous son. In the heavens above dwell Jesus and John the Baptist together, then Joseph of surpassing beauty, then Idris raised to a high place, then Aaron, then Moses who weeps that this later prophet's people shall outnumber his own. Gabriel names each and each welcomes him: welcome, righteous prophet and righteous son. Higher still than any before him, the servant of God is carried up.
stops.quote: Then I was made to ascend to the second heaven... and there were Jesus, son of Mary, and John, son of Zechariah. Every time I passed a prophet he welcomed me and said: Welcome, O righteous prophet and righteous brother.

stops.name: The Lote-Tree of the Utmost Boundary, the fifty prayers brought down to five
stops.campa: At the seventh heaven Abraham leans against the Much-Frequented House, where seventy thousand angels enter each day and return no more. Beyond it stands the Lote-Tree of the Utmost Boundary, its leaves like the ears of elephants, veiled in colours no tongue can tell; here the ascent ends and the prayers are ordained: fifty each day. Passing Moses, he is sent back, and again, and again, to plead them lower, until they are five, yet counted as fifty in reward. I have asked my Lord until I am ashamed, he says, and accepts.
stops.quote: These are five prayers and they are all equal to fifty in reward, for My Word does not change. I felt ashamed to return to my Lord again.
